title: The Twin Verses and the Mind
bigQuestion: What does the Dhammapada claim about the mind, and how do its readers turn those claims into a way of living?

story.title: Two Men, One Insult
story.kicker: The same harsh words land on two men; one carries them home, and one sets them down.
paragraphs: Picture a market in a town in ancient India. A trader loses his temper and shouts at two men who bumped his stall. He calls them thieves and fools. Both men hear every word. Both walk away. It is an ordinary morning.

The first man replays the insult all the way home. He tells his wife. He lies awake adding new replies. By morning he is planning how to get even. The second man notices the sting, then lets it go. He thinks the trader is having a bad day. He sleeps.

This small scene is not in the Dhammapada. But the Dhammapada's opening chapter is built on scenes like it. Its verses come in pairs. One verse shows a mind that holds on to harm, and the next shows a mind that lets it go. The pairs are why the chapter is called the Twin Verses.

The Dhammapada is a collection of 423 short verses in 26 chapters. It is among the most translated Buddhist texts. In this chapter you will read its first chapter and its chapter on the mind in F. Max Muller's 1881 translation, and compare his wording with modern versions.
story.think: The two men heard the same words. What made their nights different?

lessons.title: A Book of Verses
lessons.mainIdea: The Dhammapada is a Pali collection of 423 verses in 26 chapters, loved across Buddhist traditions.
reading: The *Dhammapada* sits in the Khuddaka Nikaya, the Minor Collection of the Pali Canon. Its name joins dhamma, teaching or truth, with pada, which can mean path, step, word or verse. So the title can be read as Verses of the Dhamma or Path of the Dhamma. Translators choose, and both readings fit.

The collection has 423 verses in 26 chapters, each gathered around a theme: the mind, flowers, the fool, the wise, anger, the Buddha. Scholars think it was compiled from older sayings, many of which also appear elsewhere in the canon. Related collections survive in other languages, such as the Gandhari Dharmapada and the Sanskrit Udanavarga.

Theravada monks and laypeople memorize its verses, and children in Sri Lanka and Myanmar often learn them early. F. Max Muller's translation appeared in Sacred Books of the East volume 10 in 1881 and is in the public domain. Many modern translations exist, by Narada Thera, Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Gil Fronsdal and others.

words.d: a Pali collection of 423 verses in 26 chapters; the title means verses or path of the Dhamma
the Minor Collection of the Pali Canon, which holds the Dhammapada and the Jatakas
a Pali word meaning path, step, word or verse

lessons.title: Verses and Their Stories
lessons.mainIdea: A Pali commentary tells a story behind each verse, and Buddhist teachers often teach the verse through its story.
reading: The verses stand alone, but Theravada tradition does not read them alone. A commentary called the Dhammapada Atthakatha, traditionally credited to Buddhaghosa in the fifth century CE, gives a story for each verse. The story tells when and why the Buddha is said to have spoken it.

For verse 1, the commentary tells of Cakkhupala, a blind monk who walked at night and stepped on insects without seeing them. Other monks complained. The Buddha, in the story, says he had no intention to kill, so he did no wrong. The story links the verse's claim about mind to the idea of *intention*.

E.W. Burlingame translated these stories as Buddhist Legends in 1921. Scholars see the stories as later than the verses. Buddhist teachers still use them because a story makes a short verse easier to remember and apply. A close reader can ask: does the story narrow the verse, or open it up?

words.d: a later text that explains an earlier one, verse by verse
cetana: the will or purpose behind an action, which Buddhist texts treat as the heart of karma
a fifth-century CE monk-scholar in Sri Lanka credited with many Pali commentaries

check.why: The story stresses that he had no intention to kill.

check.q: How do scholars date the commentary stories compared with the verses?
choices: The stories are later than the verses

check.why: Scholars see the commentary, credited to the fifth century CE, as later than the verses.

lessons.title: Mind Comes First
lessons.mainIdea: Verse 1 claims that what we are comes from our thoughts, and that suffering follows an evil thought.
reading: The Dhammapada opens with a claim about the mind. Muller renders it: all that we are is the result of what we have thought. The verse goes on: if a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.

The simile is concrete. An ox pulls a cart. The wheel rolls in its tracks and cannot turn aside. In the same way, the verse says, pain follows a person who acts from a harmful mind. Buddhist teachers read this as a teaching on *karma*: actions shaped by intention bring results that follow the actor.

The Pali behind the English is short: manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha manomaya. Muller made it a sentence about what we are. Modern translators often write that mind precedes all mental states, mind is their chief, they are mind-made. The word *manas*, mind, is the key. What it governs, dhamma, is harder to pin down.

words.d: the Pali and Sanskrit word for mind, the key word in verse 1
intentional action and its results; kamma in Pali
a comparison using 'as' or 'like'

lessons.title: The Twin of Verse 1
lessons.mainIdea: Verse 2 mirrors verse 1: happiness follows a pure thought like a shadow that never leaves.
reading: Verse 2 repeats verse 1 almost word for word, with two changes. The evil thought becomes a pure thought. And the image changes. Muller renders it: if a man speaks or acts with a pure thought, happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him.

Compare the two images. The wheel follows the ox with effort and grinding. The shadow follows a walker quietly and never falls away. One image is heavy, the other light. Readers note that the verse pairs match their images to their themes. The whole first chapter is built this way: twenty verses, mostly in *twin* pairs.

The pairing is a teaching method. A reader sees one path and its result, then the other path and its result, side by side. The structure invites comparison without a long argument. It also aids memory, as repetition does in the suttas. Many Buddhist children learn verses 1 and 2 together as a single lesson.

words.d: Yamaka Vagga: the first chapter of the Dhammapada, built of paired verses
repeating a sentence pattern with a change, so two ideas can be compared
a picture in words, such as the wheel or the shadow

lessons.title: He Abused Me
lessons.mainIdea: Verses 3 and 4 say hatred lasts in those who replay wrongs and ends in those who do not.
reading: Verse 3 puts words in a hurt person's mouth. In Muller's translation: he abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me. Then it says that in those who harbour such thoughts, hatred will never cease. Verse 4 is its twin: in those who do not harbour such thoughts, hatred will cease.

The key word is harbour. The verse does not say the wrongs did not happen. It speaks about holding on to them. A harbor keeps a ship safe and still. A mind that harbors a grievance keeps it safe too, and keeps it from sailing away. This is the first man in the chapter's opening scene.

Buddhist teachers often connect these verses to *anger* and to the practice of letting go. Some readers raise a question: does this ask victims to stay silent about harm? Modern Buddhist teachers answer in different ways. Many say the verse is about the inner hold of hatred, not about giving up justice or safety.

words.d: in Muller's translation, to hold on to a thought and keep it
a wrong a person feels was done to them
kodha in Pali; one of the harmful states the Dhammapada warns against

choices: It is the twin: hatred ceases in those who do not harbour such thoughts

lessons.title: An Old Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Verse 5 states that hatred does not end by hatred but by love, which it calls an old rule.
reading: Verse 5 is perhaps the most quoted line in the Dhammapada. Muller renders it: for hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule. The Pali word he translates as love is averena, which literally means by non-hatred.

Translators differ here. Muller chose love. Others write by non-enmity, by kindness or by *metta*, loving-kindness. Non-hatred is a negative word: it names the absence of something. Love is positive: it names a presence. The difference matters for what the verse asks. Is it asking a person to stop hating, or to start loving?

The commentary story tells of two women who harmed each other's children through many lives, until the Buddha taught them this verse. The phrase old rule, sanantana dhamma, suggests a law that always holds. Buddhist teachers link the verse to peace work. It has been read aloud at events including a 1951 peace conference, where Sri Lanka's J.R. Jayewardene quoted it.

words.d: the Pali word in verse 5: by non-hatred; Muller renders it 'by love'
loving-kindness; goodwill toward all beings
lasting hostility between people or groups

lessons.title: The Fletcher's Arrow
lessons.mainIdea: Chapter 3 compares training the mind to a fletcher straightening an arrow.
reading: Chapter 3, verses 33 to 43, is the Citta Vagga, the chapter on thought or mind. Here the word is *citta*, another Pali word for mind, often linked with feeling and mood. The chapter opens with a craftsman. Muller renders it: as a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought.

A fletcher made arrows. He heated a shaft and bent it until it flew true. The image says the mind is like raw wood: bent, but workable. It needs skill and patience. The verse calls thought difficult to guard and difficult to hold back. It does not call it bad. It calls it unsteady.

Verse 34 adds a second image: the mind trembles like a fish taken from the water and thrown on dry ground. Buddhist teachers read the chapter as describing how minds behave and saying they can be trained. The chapter describes; it does not give step-by-step instructions. Those are found in meditation manuals and taught in practice communities.

words.d: a Pali word for mind or heart, including mood and feeling
a person who makes arrows
bhavana: the Buddhist idea of developing the mind over time

lessons.title: A Tamed Mind
lessons.mainIdea: Verses 35 to 37 say a tamed and guarded mind brings happiness.
reading: Verse 35, in Muller's words, says it is good to tame the mind, which is difficult to hold in and flighty. A tamed mind, it says, brings happiness. Verse 36 adds that the wise should guard their thoughts, for they are hard to see and very artful. Verse 37 says those who control the mind will be free from the bonds of Mara.

*Mara* is a figure in Buddhist texts. The suttas present him as a tempter who tried to stop the Buddha's awakening. Many Buddhist teachers also read Mara as a name for the forces of craving, fear and death. The Dhammapada often uses him this way, as the one whose bonds a trained mind escapes.

The verb tame, danta, is used for horses and elephants. Pali texts often compare mind training to training an animal, patient and steady. The chapter's claims can be compared with other traditions. The Book of Proverbs, for instance, says one who rules his spirit is better than one who takes a city (Proverbs 16:32).

words.d: in Buddhist texts, the tempter who opposes awakening; also read as craving, fear and death
danta: to train, as a horse or elephant is trained
to watch over and protect, as the Dhammapada urges for thoughts

look.title: Taming as an Image
look.text: The Pali texts compare the mind to a wild elephant or horse. A trainer does not fight the animal. The trainer works day after day until it walks calmly. Verse 35 says a tamed mind brings happiness.
look.prompt: What does the animal image suggest about how Buddhist texts picture change: sudden or slow? Explain.

check.q: What does verse 35 say a tamed mind brings?
check.why: Muller: a tamed mind brings happiness.

check.q: Who is Mara in Buddhist texts?
check.why: Mara tries to stop the Buddha's awakening and stands for craving and death.

check.q: Which verse from another tradition makes a similar claim about ruling oneself?
check.why: Proverbs 16:32 praises one who rules his spirit over one who takes a city.

lessons.title: Mind as Friend or Enemy
lessons.mainIdea: Verses 42 and 43 say an ill-directed mind does more harm than an enemy, and a well-directed mind more good than family.
reading: The chapter ends with a strong pair. Verse 42 says that whatever harm a hater or an enemy may do, a wrongly directed mind will do greater harm. Verse 43 says that neither mother, father nor any relative can do as much good as a well-directed mind. It closes the chapter.

These verses rank the mind above outside forces. That can sound harsh. It seems to put all responsibility on the person. Buddhist teachers often read it more gently: outside events are real, but how the mind meets them shapes much of what follows. This is the second man in the opening scene.

The pair also closes the chapter as the twin verses began it: with *mind* as the source. A close reader notices how the Dhammapada builds its argument. It gives no long proof. It stacks images and pairs until the reader sees the pattern. This is a *didactic* style, meant to teach through repetition and memorable lines.

words.d: in the Dhammapada, citta or manas: the thinking, feeling center of a person
meant to teach a lesson
aimed in a good direction; the Dhammapada's phrase for a trained mind

check.why: A didactic text aims to teach a lesson.

lessons.title: Muller and a Modern Version
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing Muller's 1881 wording with modern translations shows how translators shape a verse's meaning.
reading: Muller worked in the 1870s, as one of the first Europeans to translate the Dhammapada into English. His English is formal and sometimes old-fashioned: harbour, listeth, unto. He also chose to read verse 1 as a claim about all that we are, a broad, almost philosophical line.

Modern translators often stay closer to the Pali shape. Many render verse 1 like this: mind precedes all mental states; mind is their chief; they are mind-made. Here, what the mind leads is mental states, dhamma in a narrow sense. That is a smaller claim than all that we are. Translators such as Narada Thera and Acharya Buddharakkhita read it this way.

Neither translation is simply right. Each makes choices about a word, dhamma, that has many meanings. A careful student names the translator, notes the choice, and asks what a reader of each would take away. The Pali stays the same. The *translation* opens one window on it at a time.

words.d: a version of a text in another language, shaped by the translator's choices
a Pali word with many senses: teaching, truth, a mental state or a thing
the way a translator puts a word or line into a new language

lessons.title: One Book, Many Readers
lessons.mainIdea: Theravada monks, Western readers and modern teachers have each used the Dhammapada in their own ways.
reading: In Theravada lands, the Dhammapada is a school text and a source of sermons. A monk giving a talk may recite a verse in Pali, then tell its commentary story. Laypeople may know dozens of verses by heart. In this setting the verses are part of a living practice of *merit* and moral training.

In nineteenth-century Europe and America, the Dhammapada was one of the first Buddhist texts people read. Muller's version made it a classic. It became a favorite of writers seeking universal wisdom. Some of these readers set aside the Buddhist setting of the verses.

Modern teachers in Asian and American communities use the Dhammapada in classes, at retreats and in prisons. Some scholars caution against reading it as a set of quotes cut off from the tradition that kept it. A close reader holds both: the verses travel easily, and they come from a particular *canon* and community.

words.d: good karma that Buddhists believe comes from good actions such as giving and learning the Dhamma
the set of texts a tradition accepts as scripture
the Buddhist tradition of Sri Lanka and much of Southeast Asia, using the Pali Canon
